method: USA Pickleball's court specification makes the playing area a 20 by 44 ft rectangle (6.10 by 13.41 m) for both singles and doubles, measured to the outside edge of the perimeter and non-volley zone lines. The net crosses the middle, so the net line sits at half the length, and the non-volley zone lines run 7 ft (2.13 m) either side of it between the two sidelines; the centerline runs from each zone line to the baseline, which leaves a service court half the width deep and half the width wide, 10 by 15 ft on a regulation court. Painted length is therefore 2L + 4W + 2 x (L/2 - 7), which is 3L + 4W - 14: 198 ft for a 44 by 20 ft court, 60.37 m for 13.41 by 6.10 m. Paint area is that length times the 2 in (5.08 cm) line width, 33 sq ft for the regulation court, and counts each crossing once rather than subtracting it. The diagonal check is the square root of length squared plus width squared, 48.33 ft between opposite corners, and the zone diagonal is the same root across a 7 ft by 20 ft zone, 21.19 ft; both square a rectangle on site, where the two tapes meet at a corner. The recommended playing surface adds 5 ft (1.52 m) beyond each sideline and 8 ft (2.44 m) behind each baseline, which gives the rulebook's 30 by 60 ft (9.14 by 18.29 m) for a regulation court and keeps the same margin around a smaller one. Net posts stand 22 ft (6.71 m) plus or minus 1 in apart between their inside faces, about 1 ft outside each sideline on a 20 ft court; the net must be 36 in at the outer sidelines and 34 in at the center, each plus or minus 0.25 in. Lengths are accepted from 20 to 60 ft (6 to 18.3 m) and widths from 10 to 40 ft (3 to 12.2 m); a size other than 44 by 20 ft is reported as a practice court rather than refused, and the metric figures are the rulebook's rounded equivalents of dimensions that are exact in feet. This is marking arithmetic on a flat surface: it does not survey a site, square a slab, or set the rules of any competition. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.
